analysis.one_liner: Bans websites from tracking users without consent and makes personal data user property.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the User Data Protection Act; it sat in committee for the rest of the 117th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for websites to use cookies, tracking pixels, or other user data without consent, barred sites from locking out users who refuse tracking, and declared collected personal data a property right owned by the user. It set no-floor damages of 90% for users who sue, and gave enforcement to the FTC, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits. It also preempted state laws on the same subject.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, who would gain consent control over tracking, a property right in their data, and new tools to sue platforms that misuse it.

how_it_helps.text: Websites could not use cookies, collect habit or preference data, or serve targeted content without the user's consent, and could not restrict access for users who decline.
Collected data would be treated as an exclusive property right owned by the user, with platforms required to disclose what they collect and what they judge it to be worth.
Users who suffer harm could sue, with damages of no less than 90% of total harm and capped attorney's fees, and enforcement also available through the FTC and state attorneys general.

analysis.who_pays: Digital platforms, advertising companies, and data brokers that profit from tracking users and selling or sharing their information, plus compliance costs passed to consumers.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts any State law relating to its requirements, so it would have overridden stronger existing state privacy rules in the states.
The preemption limit makes this strictly weaker than comprehensive state privacy laws for users in those states.

Requiring consent for basic functions like essential cookies could add friction to everyday browsing, and the private right of action with a guaranteed 90% damages share could drive costly litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are strong for users, but the federal preemption clause would have wiped out stronger state privacy laws, so net benefit depends on state law baseline; still, the bill died without any action, so neither benefit nor cost was realized.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then its Consumer Protection subcommittee, where it stalled for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Introduced June 29, 2021 by Rep. Schweikert with no cosponsors.
Referred to House Energy and Commerce Committee on June 29, 2021, and June 30, 2021 to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Digital platforms and the adtech industry, which avoided new consent and data-property restrictions because the bill never advanced.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it stalled in committee and subcommittee without a markup or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor with no cosponsors from either party, so no clear partisan pattern is visible.

industries.note: The bill would ban tracking pixels and require consent, hitting core revenue from behavioral tracking and data sales.
Consent requirements and data property rights would curb their tracking practices and compliance costs would likely be passed to consumers.
